title: Short Stuff: Leisure Suits
summary: Short Stuff episode on leisure suits. Josh and Chuck (with Jerry sitting in for Dave) open with banter about the show's silly short-format tone, then trace leisure suit precursors: 1800s British lounge suit, 1920s American sack suit, and 1960s hippies wanting relaxed office wear. They discuss the name possibly coming from Lee jeans' "Leesure" suit, designed by Jerry Rosengarten and released around 1972, aimed at men for office wear and moms for Easter. Typical features (wide lapels, flared pants, contrasting stitching, polyester, matching vest) are described, along with pop-culture examples (Cousin Eddie, Otho in Beetlejuice, Travolta's Saturday Night Fever suit, Charlie's Angels). The suit fell out of favor quickly, became a joke, and was replaced by the 1980s power suit. Closes with the Saturday Night Fever suit's history: bought for about $100 in New Jersey, bought by Gene Siskel in 1978, sold in 1995 for $145,000, and sold at auction in 2023 for about $260,000.

segments.title: Short Stuff intro and leisure suit setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the short-format episode, joking about its silly tone and introducing leisure suits as a 1970s icon.

segments.title: Precursors to the leisure suit
segments.summary: The hosts trace early relaxed suits: 1960s hippies wanting chill office wear, 1800s British lounge suits, and 1920s American sack suits.

segments.title: Polyester origins
segments.summary: Chuck notes polyester appeared in the UK in the 1940s and became big in the US in the 1970s, when the leisure suit arrived.

segments.title: Name origin: Lee's Leesure suit
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether the name comes from Lee jeans' L-E-E-S-U-R-E suit, which Josh says was designed by Jerry Rosengarten and debuted around 1972, marketed to businessmen and mothers for Easter wear.

segments.title: Leisure suit look and styling
segments.summary: Describes the typical look: matching flared pants and shirt-style jacket, wide lapels, sometimes a vest, contrasting stitching, and white patent leather shoes.

segments.title: Pop culture leisure suits and decline
segments.summary: Examples include Cousin Eddie and Otho from Beetlejuice. Chuck says the suit was meant for office wear but became a formal-occasion or disco outfit, then a joke, and was replaced by the 1980s power suit.

segments.title: Travolta's Saturday Night Fever suit
segments.summary: The hosts cover the white suit from Saturday Night Fever: bought for about $100 in New Jersey, bought by Gene Siskel in 1978, sold in 1995 for $145,000, and sold at auction in 2023 for about $260,000.

segments.title: Charlie's Angels and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck notes women also wore pantsuit leisure suits, with Josh mentioning Charlie's Angels, then a brief joke exchange and iHeartRadio sign-off.
